synopsis: The booklet treats nuisance warnings and unnecessary braking as safety objectives: frequent interruptions can undermine trust and lead operators to ignore or disable the system [f7000, f14430, f14437]. After hard safety constraints are satisfied, tuning should balance nuisance rates, comfort, productivity loss and braking timing through constrained multi-objective optimisation, rather than pursue zero misses or zero nuisance alone [f6963, f14441, f14442]. In a seven-day NIOSH radar trial on a Caterpillar 793B, 580 alarms occurred in 618 reversals; 18% were false, 42% concerned objects already known to the driver, and 41% warranted action, with researchers finding the audible warning disabled after shifts [f14431, f14432, f14433]. Another trial reported false alarms infrequent enough that the system was not ignored, but no study defines an acceptable false-alarm rate for off-road operators [f14434, f14439]. The proposed way to establish practical limits is an operator clinic measuring acceptance thresholds by scenario, with escalation or stopping if the design cannot meet those thresholds; useful tuning measures include unnecessary warnings or interventions per operating hour, loading cycle and reverse maneuver [f10966, f10967, f10968, f14440].
